## It wasn't great

So for the past 2 years or so, I've been making somewhat voluntarily some simplifications about what it means to train a model.

That won't cut it anymore...

## Train, Validation, Test

If you look at the RLCS package demos, you will see that I separate a Train/Test set for supervised learning.

The better way (right way?) to do this is train, validation, test.

In train, you learn, in validation you do exercise exams, in test you do real world testing.

In theory, validation can be used for further tuning.

## More configurations, more sets

After the above, and considering stratified cross-validation, one ends up training with "a few datasets out of each dataset". You do machine learning for Iris, but you try different separations of samples.

And then, each algorithm has potentially several more-or-less optional parameters. The famous hyperparameters. For example, Tree depth in Partitioning Trees, or number of trees for Random Forest, number of layers in Neural Networks, etc..

And then some algorithms have some stochastic property, RLCS being a good example. So to make sure it was a realistic result, for these you might want to run several times the training, even on the exact same datasets! You just use different seeds for your RNG.

What do you end up with?

Hundreds, **maybe thousands** of trainings/validations/testings for one dataset. That is, if you want serious results.

And now with the PhD, I've got to be serious alright.

## So...

Processing power and parallel evaluations are going to be helpful. Thank goodness I have access to good resources, now with the University too!
